prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms held at a magic wavelength enable frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part B004 configuration for Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye and have not changed it since round 1. The round-1 exchange sharpened the case rather than altering it. What the lattice clock did is specific: Katori's magic-wavelength trap removes the conflict between holding many neutral atoms tightly and leaving the clock transition unperturbed, and Ye's group showed what that idea could deliver, with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and control of many-body effects in a degenerate gas. Both halves have been reproduced and compared across laboratories for about two decades, so there is no open question about whether the result is real. As a builder of instruments I judge it as a measurement advance: a new regime of what can be measured and how well, which feeds tests of constants, millimetre-scale relativistic redshift and dark-sector searches. The two names map onto the proposal and the record realisation. On the chair's question about the second, I treat its redefinition as supporting evidence only and not a condition; the scientific case is complete without it. I also want the record to show that I am relying on the science and the credit, not on the seven-of-eight count, which I do not count as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The distinctness judgement is still not proven, and I should say so plainly. The 2005 prize (frequency comb) and the 2012 prize (control of single trapped ions) are adjacent, and Danielsson and Olsson are right that the lattice clock can be read as the next refinement of a line already honoured. I answer that the new element is the neutral-atom ensemble in a magic-wavelength lattice, which neither prize covered, but this is a judgement, not a demonstration. Credit is the second weakness: I cannot verify from the supplied record the roles of Takamoto and other Sr-lattice colleagues, or the priority of PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN groups, and a two-name prize leaves real contributors out. The third is that this is a prize for an instrument and a measurement capability, which Danielsson weighs less than a clue found in nature, and he may be right that IceCube becomes the stronger case within a year or two. None of these outweighs the combination of originality, confirmation and clean attribution for me, but they are the reasons a colleague could vote differently.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the citation should address Takamoto and other Sr-lattice colleagues, and discloses a doctoral research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, Ye's institution.
responses.response: On credit, I would not change the names: the supplied record does not let me verify a priority claim that would displace Katori or Ye, and I will not rewrite a credit from recollection. I would instead word the citation around the lattice-clock concept and its record realisation, not around optical clocks in general, so that it does not claim the whole field; my citation does this. On disclosure, a historical research stay in a laboratory associated with a different institution than the credited person's own group, with no documented personal or collaborative tie to Katori or Ye, is in my view adequately handled by the disclosure he has already made. I do not regard it as requiring recusal, and I would only ask that he confirm that no co-authorship or ongoing collaboration with Ye's group exists, which his profile does not suggest.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the lattice clock is a new regime and not a refinement, but fears we choose the more comfortable attribution over the more consequential discovery (B032), and says I should not drive the IceCube case.
responses.response: I accept the second point and will not drive B032; my field of experimental astroparticle physics is close enough that I would defer to colleagues on its weight and consider recusal if it became the leading option. On the first, your argument that the lattice adds a large neutral ensemble free of motional shifts, giving stability and accuracy together, is the best statement of distinctness in the record, and I adopt it. I do not think we are choosing comfort over consequence: the atom-by-atom allocation in IceCube cannot be settled from the evidence here, as you yourself concede, and a prize whose credited names we cannot defend would be worse for the science than waiting. I agree that B032 should return if the source associations firm up and the roles can be documented.

responses.point: Olsson presses Mehlig and me on prior recognition, saying the 2005 prize can be read as showing that the clock line has already been honoured, and asks Johansson whether his eighth place is a physics or a recognition judgement.
responses.response: I accept that the 2005 prize cuts both ways, and I should not have cited it as support for timing. It supports only the narrow claim that the comb, a recognised tool, made optical frequency counting possible, whereas the lattice clock is a separate invention built on it. So the question is whether a new invention in an honoured area can be prized, and the committee has done that before. What would persuade me otherwise is a showing that Katori's lattice idea was anticipated or that the stability gain came mainly from the laser and comb technology already prized, and nobody has shown that. I also thank you for setting aside B010 for maturity and credit; I agree that was a judgement about timing and not about the physics.

responses.point: Johansson wants the citation to avoid wording that depends on the second being redefined and to avoid claiming the whole clock field, and in round 1 referred to Ye being credited under other candidate lines.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and have changed my citation to follow it: it names the lattice clock and the 10^-18 level, and it makes no reference to timekeeping in general or to the redefinition of the second. On Ye, the shortlist shows him only under B004, so I do not see a balance problem from other lines, and I would ask you to confirm that you meant that and not another candidate. I also note that you moved from eighth to first and said the earlier ranking reflected your field's pull and not a weakness of the candidate; I take that at face value and agree that a theory-only B023 is a weaker second step.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B010 for MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, argues that an open pairing mechanism has not historically stopped recognition of an established phenomenon, and keeps B004 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I take the argument seriously: the correlated states are reproduced across groups and the discovery honoured is their existence, not the glue. I still do not move B010 ahead of B004. The contested credit (Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, the 2018 first author and parallel experimental groups) and an eight-year-old field leave a larger risk of a citation that ages badly. On your side I agree that dropping Bistritzer would be hard to defend, so if B010 returns I would support the three-name version. I would ask you directly: if the committee settles on B004, is there anything in the record that would stop you from supporting it as a single-part prize, and what would you want to see on credit for B010 to be ready next year?

uncertainties: Whether the lattice clock is judged distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I regard it as distinct but the argument is a judgement.
Whether Takamoto and other Sr-lattice and Yb contributors, or the groups at PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN, hold priority claims that would alter the credited pair; I cannot verify this from the record.
The relative weight of Katori's idea against Ye's realisation within a two-name credit.
Whether B032 will be clearer in a year or two, and whether three defensible IceCube names exist.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent for B004 from my profile: my documented connections (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH) include neither Katori nor Ye. I am close to experimental astroparticle physics, so I would not drive B032 and would consider recusal from decisions on it if it became the leading option. I note Kroll's disclosure of his stay in Hall's laboratory and do not regard it as requiring any step beyond disclosure.
